angle: No seat limits, purely usage-based, and a 20-person team: why a full sales process on every signup is impossible
post_first_line: A team of 20-something can't sell to everyone.
linkedin_post:
A team of 20-something can't sell to everyone.

Dima Khlopkov explained why a full sales process on every signup breaks down, and what changed the pricing model.

The team runs a lean operation, 20-something people, against a high volume of incoming signups and leads. Running a full sales process on every one of them is impossible.

So the model has no limits. It's purely usage-based.

The approach today is a hybrid. It changed about 4 months ago, maybe 5.

The constraint wasn't the product or the market. It was headcount versus inbound volume.

When the team can't touch everyone, the pricing model has to do part of the selling.

Where does your sales process break at volume?

lesson.title: Let your pricing model absorb what your team can't
takeaways: A lean team of 20-something can't run a full sales process on every signup.
Usage-based pricing with no limits lets people get started without a sales touch.
A hybrid approach lets sales effort go where it's needed, and the model can change as you learn. This one changed about 4 months ago.
lesson.exercise: Compare last month's inbound signups to the number of people your team can realistically work. Decide which signups get a full sales process and which get a usage-based path.

angle: From easy to hard PLG signals: from 30-day inactivity to a power user who changes jobs and champions you at the new company
linkedin_post:
30 days inactive, then a login.

That's the easiest PLG signal. The hardest one is much more valuable.

Dima Khlopkov laid out how signals range from very simple to advanced and hard to get.

At the simple end: a user goes inactive for some time, then logs in again after around 30 days.

At the hard end: a power user switches jobs, lands in a new workspace, and starts trying out Gumloop, even on a free package.

That second signal matters because the team can approach that person while they're excited. They can champion the product in the new org.

But Dima's advice is not to overthink signals. Implement whatever comes to mind first, then iterate across different places and sequences.

Start with the obvious one. Get it live. Refine it later.

lesson.title: Start simple, then climb the PLG signal ladder
takeaways: PLG signals range from simple (a login after around 30 days of inactivity) to advanced and hard to get.
A power user who changes jobs and tries the product in a new workspace can become a champion in the new org.
Overthinking signals is a mistake; implement what comes to mind first and iterate across places and sequences.
lesson.exercise: List five PLG signals you could track, ranked from easiest to hardest. Implement the easiest one this week, then add one harder signal after you see how it performs.

angle: A 3-tier outbound system: manual for top accounts, semi-automated in the middle, fully automated for the rest
post_first_line: Three tiers. Three levels of automation.
linkedin_post:
Three tiers. Three levels of automation.

Dima Khlopkov doesn't run one outbound motion for every account. The split is where the system gets interesting.

Tier 1 is the most manual. The GTM team writes the email by hand and refines it. Sometimes there's a link between our head of sales or a founder and that individual. That's a detail worth mentioning, and it's impossible to gather with an AI agent and a web search.

Tier 2 is semi-automated. Emails run automatically, but the LinkedIn steps stay manual. The goal is to diversify how those accounts get touched.

Tier 3 is a fully automated sequence.

The point is to match the effort to the account instead of treating every account the same. Human time goes where human context actually changes the message.

Where do you draw the line between manual and automated?
carousel: Slide 1: Stop running one outbound motion for every account.
Slide 2: Split your accounts into three tiers of automation.
Slide 3: Tier 1: manual steps, with hand-refined emails.
Slide 4: Use context an AI agent can't find, like a founder connection.
Slide 5: Tier 2: automated emails, manual LinkedIn steps.
Slide 6: Mixing channels diversifies how those accounts get touched.
Slide 7: Tier 3: a fully automated sequence.
Slide 8: Spend human effort where human context changes the message.

lesson.title: Build a 3-tier outbound system
takeaways: Tier 1 is manual: hand-refined emails that use context an AI agent and a web search can't gather, like a link between your founders or head of sales and the contact.
Tier 2 is semi-automated: automated emails, with manual LinkedIn steps to diversify the touch.
Tier 3 is a fully automated sequence for the remaining accounts.
lesson.exercise: Sort your target accounts into three tiers. For each tier, write down which steps stay manual and which are automated. Then, for tier 1, list any personal connections between your team and those contacts.

angle: Timing beats messaging: reach people the week they try your product, and name-drop a teammate
post_first_line: Timing beats messaging at every level.
linkedin_post:
Timing beats messaging at every level.

Dima Khlopkov has a simple rule for who to reach out to first, and it has nothing to do with copy.

In Dima Khlopkov's view, the best moment to talk to someone is right after they try your product. They just signed up for Gumloop, they're excited about the platform, and they're in the best state possible to chat.

The message itself stays very simple. Personalize based on role: GTM teams are using Gumloop for this and that, or marketing teams are using Gumloop for this and that.

Then name-drop people.

Dima Khlopkov's take: name-dropping is a different level of personalization, because you can't really source that information from the internet.

So the order of operations is: get the timing right, keep the message simple, and add the one detail nobody can scrape.

What's the best trigger you've timed outreach around?
carousel: Slide 1: Timing beats messaging at every level.
Slide 2: Reach people right after they try your product.
Slide 3: They're excited, and in the best state to chat.
Slide 4: Keep the message simple. Personalize by role.
Slide 5: GTM teams use us for this. Marketing teams, for that.
Slide 6: Then name-drop a teammate or a person they know.
Slide 7: That detail can't be sourced from the internet.
Slide 8: Right moment, simple message, one unscrapable detail.

lesson.title: Win on timing, then add the detail nobody can scrape
takeaways: The best moment to reach someone is right after they try your product, while they're excited.
A simple message personalized by role is enough when timing is right.
Name-dropping people is a deeper level of personalization because the information can't be sourced from the internet.
lesson.exercise: Pick one recent product-trial trigger. Write a two-sentence message personalized by role, add one real name of a teammate or peer, and send it within the same week.

angle: 10-12% reply rates from acting on one LinkedIn signal: who viewed your founder's profile
linkedin_post:
10 to 12% reply rates. From outbound.

It came from acting on one kind of signal, and most teams ignore it.

Dima Khlopkov noticed that when a prospect recently viewed the founder's profile, viewed the company's profile, or engaged with the company's content, Gumloop was top of mind for them.

That is the best time to reach out.

So the team combined inbound and outbound. They act on LinkedIn-based signals and keep inbound-led outbound flows, without being too pushy and while still reaching out at the right time.

The result: they can keep reply rates at 10 to 12%.

The outreach isn't cold anymore. The prospect already raised a hand, just quietly.

Slide 2: The trigger was a LinkedIn profile view

lesson.title: Inbound-led outbound: time outreach to LinkedIn signals
takeaways: Profile views of the founder or company and content engagement show a prospect has your brand top of mind.
The best time to reach out is right after those signals, without being pushy.
Combining inbound signals with outbound flows kept reply rates at 10 to 12%.
lesson.exercise: List the LinkedIn signals you can see this week (founder profile views, company profile views, content engagement). Pick one, then message the people who triggered it within a day.

angle: What's a good positive reply rate? Product signals can run 4x the norm
post_first_line: Product signals can drive 4x reply rates.
linkedin_post:
Product signals can drive 4x reply rates.

But the answer to "what's a good reply rate" starts with "it depends."

Quintin Smith has been digging into this data at Unify. The most honest answer is that positive reply rate is determined by the type of signal you use. It keeps climbing as you combine and layer signals.

Here's the range Quintin Smith shared:

Positive replies on a standard motion: anywhere from 0.2 to 1%.

Replies in general on a standard motion: 1 to 3%.

Product signals specifically: the reply rate can be 4x higher than a typical positive reply rate.

The reason is simple. Those are your warmest accounts.

So before you benchmark your numbers, check which signal is behind the outreach. A "bad" reply rate may just be a cold list, not bad messaging.

What reply rate are you seeing on your best signal?
carousel: Slide 1: What's a good positive reply rate? It depends.
Slide 2: Signal type largely determines your reply rate.
Slide 3: Layering signals pushes the numbers even higher.
Slide 4: Standard positive replies: roughly 0.2 to 1%.
Slide 5: Standard replies overall: 1 to 3% is typical.
Slide 6: Product signals can hit 4x a typical positive reply rate.
Slide 7: Why? Those are your warmest accounts.
Slide 8: Benchmark by signal, not by one blended number.

lesson.title: Benchmark reply rates by signal type
takeaways: Positive reply rate depends heavily on the type of signal behind the outreach, and it climbs as signals are layered.
Standard benchmarks: 0.2 to 1% positive replies, 1 to 3% for replies in general.
Product signals can produce a reply rate around 4x a typical positive reply rate because those accounts are the warmest.
lesson.exercise: Split your last month of outbound by signal source (product signal, other signals, no signal). Calculate the positive reply rate for each and compare it to the 0.2 to 1% standard range.
